name: Corn, sweet
summary: How Filipino farmers grow sweet corn for fresh ears sold in markets and by the roadside. Most use hybrid seed bought each crop and pick the ears about two and a half months after planting.
season: Grown all year where water is available. Rainfed growers plant at the start of the rains, around May to June, and many plant again from October to January, when there is less disease and the ears fill well with watering.
material: Hybrid seed bought new every crop. The seed is small and wrinkled and needs moist, warm soil and a shallow planting. Some growers sow in seedling trays and set the young plants out after about two weeks to save on costly seed.
spacing: Rows about 75 cm apart with one plant every 20 to 25 cm.
water: Needs steady moisture. In the dry season growers run water into the furrows about once a week, more often in sandy soil, and never let the field dry out from tasseling to harvest.
fertilizer: Chicken manure at land preparation if available, complete fertilizer (14 14 14) in the furrow at planting, and urea (46 0 0) at about three weeks before hilling up. Some growers give a little more urea at tasseling.
care: Off barring at about two weeks and hilling up at about three to four weeks, with hand weeding in the rows. Growers check the whorls often for fall armyworm and corn borer, which hit sweet corn harder than field corn.
harvest: Sweet corn is picked fresh, about 65 to 75 days after planting, when the silks are dry and brown and the kernels are full and milky. The ears are sold or cooked within a day.

steps.title: Plow and harrow
steps.how: Plow once and harrow two times to get a fine, loose seedbed. Many growers spread chicken manure before the last harrowing.

steps.title: Fertilizer in the furrow
steps.how: Drop complete fertilizer (14 14 14) in the furrow and cover it with a little soil.

steps.title: Plant the seed shallow
steps.how: Drop one seed every 20 to 25 cm and cover it with only 2 to 3 cm of moist soil, since sweet corn seed rots if buried deep in wet ground.

steps.title: Water after planting
steps.how: If the soil is dry, run water into the furrows or water by hand so the seed comes up evenly.

steps.title: Replant the misses
steps.how: Replant empty hills within the first week so the plants ripen together.

steps.title: Off barring and weeding
steps.how: Plow lightly between the rows with the soil thrown away from the plants, then hand pull the weeds in the rows.

steps.title: Look into the whorls
steps.how: Check the whorls for fall armyworm and corn borer damage every few days, since sweet corn is their favorite.

steps.title: Side dress urea
steps.how: Drop urea (46 0 0) beside the plants on moist soil.

steps.title: Hill up
steps.how: Plow toward the rows to cover the fertilizer and firm the plants against wind.

steps.title: Water well through silking
steps.how: Keep the soil moist from tasseling until the ears fill. Dry soil now gives ears with missing kernels.

steps.title: Pick the fresh ears
steps.how: Harvest about 18 to 22 days after the silks appear, when the silks are brown and dry and a pressed kernel gives milky juice. Pick in the cool early morning.

steps.title: Sell or cool the same day
steps.how: Keep the picked ears in the shade and get them to the buyer the same day, since the sweetness fades quickly in the heat.

mistakes: Burying the seed too deep in wet soil, so much of it rots before it comes up.
Planting next to field corn that flowers at the same time, which makes the kernels starchy and less sweet.
Letting the soil dry out at silking, which gives ears with gaps.
Picking too late, when the kernels have turned doughy and starchy.
Leaving picked ears in the sun for hours before selling.
better: Buy fresh seed of a variety suited to your season and plant into moist, fine soil.
Keep sweet corn away from other corn, or plant it so it flowers at least two weeks apart.
Feed by a soil test and split the nitrogen into two or three doses.
Scout every few days for fall armyworm and act while the larvae are small.
Plant in small batches every two weeks so you have ears to sell over a longer time.

watering.traditional: Sweet corn growers water more than field corn growers, because the ears sell on their size and sweetness. In the dry season most run water into the furrows about once a week, or water by hose on small plots, and never let the field dry from tasseling to harvest.
watering.method: Furrow watering from a pump or canal on bigger fields, and a hose or watering can on small plots. Water in the cool early morning or late afternoon.
watering.rainfed: Plant at the start of the rains so the ears fill during the wet weeks, and on raised ridges if the field is low. Mulch with rice straw to keep moisture between rains, and plant only what you can water if the rains stop early.
watering.dryseason: The dry season crop from October to January needs watering about once a week, more often on sandy soil and in the hot months. Water when the soil a few centimeters down feels dry or the leaves start to roll before noon, and never miss a watering from tasseling to picking.
watering.wet: Make ridges and keep the furrow ends open so rain drains away, since standing water yellows and stunts the plants. Wet weather also brings more leaf diseases and rotting of the ear tips, so do not water on top of the rain.

schedule.often: Water right after planting if the soil is dry, then every few days until the seedlings are up
schedule.amount: Enough to wet the soil around the seed, never soggy
schedule.why: Sweet corn seed is weak and rots in soggy soil, but needs moisture to come up evenly.

schedule.often: About once a week in dry weather, more often on sandy soil
schedule.amount: One furrow watering, or a slow soaking along the row by hose on small plots
schedule.why: Even growth now gives plants that tassel together.

schedule.often: About once a week, and soon after the urea and hilling up
schedule.amount: Fill the furrows and let the water soak in
schedule.why: The plant is building the leaves and stalk that will feed the ear.

schedule.often: Keep the soil moist all the time, watering at least once a week in dry weather and more often on sandy soil
schedule.amount: A full furrow watering each time
schedule.why: Dry soil now gives short ears with missing kernels and less sweetness.

schedule.often: Keep the soil just moist until the ears are picked
schedule.amount: A light watering only if the soil is dry
schedule.why: Moist soil keeps the kernels juicy and tender up to picking.

critical: Tasseling and silking, about day 45 to 55: a dry spell now leaves gaps of missing kernels on the ear.
Ear filling, about day 55 to 68: the kernels fill with sugar and water, so drought gives small, less sweet ears.
Coming up: the seedbed must stay moist until the seedlings are out.

signs.dry: Leaves roll in the morning and look gray green, the silks dry before they catch pollen, and the ears come out short with gaps and few kernels at the tip.
signs.wet: Yellow lower leaves, pale stunted plants in the low spots, and seed that rots before it comes up.

better: Drip lines along the rows with rice straw mulch use far less water than furrows and keep the soil evenly moist through silking.
Plant in blocks a week or two apart only as fast as you can water them, so no block is short of water at silking.
